    According to recent reports, the annual GM Meetings came and went this week with only one significant transaction: Evan Phillips signed with the Braves. Phillips, our 34th-ranked free agent, received a three-year deal worth $35 million. He'll replace Raisel Iglesias in Atlanta's bullpen and pair with Robert Suarez at the end of the game. The Braves could still re-sign Iglesias too, I suppose.

    Otherwise, the GM Meetings brought a lot of rumors -- A LOT of rumors -- and presumably the groundwork was laid for moves that could be completed later this offseason. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and the notable offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

    It has been revealed that the Rangers are among the teams with interest in Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, reports The Athletic. Sato primarily played third base for the Hanshin Tigers, though he does not stand out defensively, and could land at first base or in the corner outfield in MLB. Texas could stand to upgrade at first base and could always slot Sato in at DH as well.

    Sources indicate that we ranked Sato as the fourth-best free agent available and the best free agent position player. The reigning Triple Crown winner in Japan hit .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs in 2026. Sato, 28 in March, has some similarities to Munetaka Murakami as a lefty with massive power and swing-and-miss concerns, though Sato is a much more aggressive hitter and won't walk as much as Murakami.

    With Miguel Rojas retired, the Dodgers are looking to add a right-handed hitting infielder, according to The Athletic. Mookie Betts and Max Muncy are entrenched on the left side of the infield. Tommy Edman, a switch-hitter, is penciled in at second base, with fellow switch-hitter Alex Freeland next in line as depth. Freeland has not hit much in his limited MLB time, however.

    According to recent reports, this is not a great free agent class overall, but it does feature several utility infielders who hit right-handed. Among them are Mauricio Dubón, Ha-Seong Kim, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Edmundo Sosa. Glovemen Oswald Peraza (Angels) and Jared Triolo (Pirates) are potential trade targets. Rojas was a very productive role player for Los Angeles. He won't be so easy to replace.

    The Padres are receiving calls about catchers Luis Campusano and Freddy Fermin, according to the San Diego Union-Tribune. Top prospect Ethan Salas was called up in September and became the youngest catcher to appear in the postseason in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series. Salas is the future behind the plate, making Campusano or Fermin (or perhaps both) expendable.

    In a recent development, campusano and Fermin are very different players. Campusano is a bat-first catcher who might be worth keeping given his age (28) and the fact that the Padres could slot him at DH. That said, those same qualities make him appealing to other teams. Fermin, 31, is a terrific defender who hasn't hit much the last few years. The Padres need pitching and could deal a catcher or two for an arm or two.

    Samsung Lions outfielder Ja-Wook Koo has hired a newly introduced agent and is looking to make the jump to MLB, reports MLB.com. Koo, a 10-time All-Star and this year's Korean Series MVP, has been among the best hitters in the Korea Baseball Organization the last few years. The 33-year-old hit .371/.458/.581 with 15 homers and nearly as many walks (66) as strikeouts (71) in 2026.

    According to recent reports, koo's age and the fact he's a left-handed hitter in a market inundated with left-handed hitting outfielders will work against him in free agency. He has a great track record in Korea, though, including a history of high contact rates, which could make him a cheaper and more appealing target than MLB free agents like Michael Conforto, Trent Grisham, Cedric Mullins, and Daulton Varsho.

There's a real chance Skubal signs a contract worth more than $400 million in the next two weeks or so. Excluding Shohei Ohtani, who is technically a pitcher but is really a two-way player, here are the largest pitching contracts in history:.

    It has been revealed that 1. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers: $325M.

    Sources indicate that 2. Justin Verlander, Mets: $43.3M.

    Recent findings suggest that 3. Stephen Strasburg, Nationals: $245M.

    3. Zack Wheeler, Phillies: $42M.

    4. Framber Valdez, Tigers: $38.3M.

    In a recent development, something like, say, eight years at $50 million a year would give Skubal a $400 million contract that obliterates the previous pitcher records for total guarantee and average annual value. Several big-market clubs are said to be pursuing Skubal (Blue Jays, Dodgers, Mets, etc.), who is a special free agent as an in-his-prime ace. Conditions are ripe for a record deal.

    There is also a chance Skubal goes the Valdez route, or the Bo Bichette/Kyle Tucker route, and signs a short-term contract with a high annual salary. It might only be a small chance, but there is a chance. The Athletic reports the Dodgers prefer such an arrangement with Skubal. ESPN says Skubal has no interest in such a deal, though minds can always be changed.

    It has been revealed that with that in mind, here are the pros and cons of a high-dollar, short-term contract for Skubal. Keep in mind that such a contract is usually a three- or four-year deal with opt outs, not a straight one- or two-year contract, and Skubal wouldn't necessarily have to use the opt outs to re-enter free agency. He could leverage them into a latest contract to stay with his team.

    1. Maximize earnings. Plain and simple, a short-term contract would give Skubal a chance to max out his earnings by making free agency available to him again as soon as next offseason. Go out, have a typical Skubal season in 2027, and perhaps market forces push the demand even higher than it is right now. Remember that, along with a salary cap, there could be a salary floor in the future. Small-market contenders like, say, the Guardians or Rays could throw many millions at Skubal to reach the floor in the future.

    2. Chance to set more records. This ties back to the last point. Skubal already set a newly introduced salary record for an arbitration-eligible player ($32 million in 2026) and he's positioned to set a new standard for pitcher contracts this offseason. Go back into free agency in a year or two, and Skubal (and Boras) could have a chance to break his own pitcher contract record. The record itself won't be a driving factor in that decision (the money will ultimately decide things), but it would be a nice feather in his cap.

    Sources indicate that 3. Freedom to change teams. Sometimes things don't work out. I don't think Juan Soto expected to miss the postseason in the first two years of his record 15-year, $765 million contract with the Mets. It's entirely possible Skubal could find his next situation not to his liking for whatever reason. Maybe the team doesn't contend, maybe he clashes with the coaching staff, maybe he doesn't like the local breakfast taco options. There could be a million different reasons it doesn't work. A short-term, high-dollar deal would give Skubal an escape hatch and allow him to head elsewhere if things go sideways.

    Industry observers note that 1. Injury and performance risk. All things considered, Skubal is a pretty safe bet on a long-term contract, though he is a pitcher, and pitchers get hurt. It's what they do. Skubal has had three elbow surgeries, including Tommy John surgery in 2017 and a minor procedure this May. If he gets hurt again, or his performance slips for whatever reason, then he could wind up costing himself in the massive picture because he won't be able to opt out and sign a larger deal. A short-term, high-dollar contract will pay him handsomely. He won't struggle to put bread on the table. But injury/performance risk means Skubal could ultimately leave money on the table.

    Sources indicate that 2. Potential salary cap. It is possible the next CBA will include a salary cap, which could limit Skubal's market and earning potential should he go back out into free agency in a year or two (or three). It's not just the cap itself either. MLB has proposed contract limits as part of the salary cap: five years at 15% of the cap for players who change teams, or six years at 16% of the cap for players who remain with their current team. Even if MLB doesn't get a salary cap and instead the competitive balance tax system remains in place with stiffer penalties, that could cost Skubal in the future. This offseason might be his last chance to sign in a truly free market.

    #61931. Between a Lack of Stability and Connection Issues

    📅 25 Jan 2025 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2824 w)

    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Spielverlagerung ↗ Open Full Page

    Between a Lack of Stability and Connection Issues

    📅 25 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 25.01.2025 in den Kategorien Europa League mit 0 Kommentaren.
    • Industry observers note that tottenham Hotspur and TSG Hoffenheim disappoint on Thursday evening in Sinsheim, with Hoffenheim showing promising adjustments in the second half but still falling short.
    • Christian Ilzer and TSG Hoffenheim were under pressure on the penultimate matchday of the UEFA Europa League: Only a win would keep their theoretical chance of direct progression alive.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 25.01.2025 in den Kategorien Europa League mit 0 Kommentaren.

    Industry observers note that tottenham Hotspur and TSG Hoffenheim disappoint on Thursday evening in Sinsheim, with Hoffenheim showing promising adjustments in the second half but still falling short. It was a match defined by approaches and ambivalence, as both teams displayed glimpses of potential but lacked the necessary consistency and presence. (MX).

    Christian Ilzer and TSG Hoffenheim were under pressure on the penultimate matchday of the UEFA Europa League: Only a win would keep their theoretical chance of direct progression alive. The Austrian coach opted for a 4-2-2-2 formation. Oliver Baumann performed as usual as the goalkeeper, with Akpoguma and Nsoki forming the center-back duo, flanked by Jurásek on the left and Kadeřábek on the right. The double pivot consisted of Stach and Becker, while Bischof – who will soon join FC Bayern – and Hložek were deployed in the half-spaces. Up front, Morstedt and Kramarić played as a dual-striker pair.

    It has been revealed that on the opposite side, there was also significant pressure on Ange Postecoglou and Tottenham. Domestically, the team was in a difficult situation, and in the Europa League, a win was necessary to keep their chances of progressing in their own hands for the following week. The Spurs lined up in a 4-3-3 formation, with Austin in goal. Dragusin and Davies formed the central defensive pairing, while Gray and Porro occupied the full-back roles. In midfield, Maddison, Bentancur, and the young Bergvall played as central figures. The attacking line consisted of Kulusevski, Richarlison, and Son.

    Hoffenheim’s 4-4-2 Pressing System.

    The Hoffenheim pressing structure without the ball was primarily based on a 4-4-2 formation, which Ilzer had successfully used in recent weeks and also in Graz for midfield pressing. In this formation, Bischof and Hložek played as wide players, while Moerstedt and Kramarić formed the first pressing line. The ball-near striker didn’t press the ball-carrying center-back directly, but rather in a looser manner. The main focus was on controlling the diagonal dribbles of Dragusin and Davies and blocking the diagonal passing lanes into the center. Additionally, the far-side striker often took on the task of marking Bentancur, the central defensive midfielder.

    A key characteristic of Ilzer’s approach was also that the strikers often moved wide from their diagonal pressing movements, putting more pressure on the width and preventing backward passes more effectively. This approach indirectly highlighted how crucial compactness is for Ilzer’s system. Without tight distances between the lines, it was difficult for the strikers to press effectively and create double pressure. In situations where compactness was not ensured, such as in some midfield pressing moments, unfavorable 1v1 situations arose that significantly diminished the advantage of the system, as the player could directly engage in a 1v1 duel instead of a 1v2 situation with the pressing striker.

    The attempt to block diagonal movements by the pressing striker inevitably led to a drawback: Tottenham was increasingly forced to play wide. Here, Hoffenheim highlighted some ambivalence. Tottenham frequently positioned their full-backs in half-space, forcing Bischof and Hložek to track them. The issue, however, was that the width, which should have been covered by the outer midfielders in the 4-4-2 system, was insufficiently secured. This created patterns that became an increasing challenge for Hoffenheim.

    Tottenham’s Width-Based Strategy.

    Postecoglou likely recognized the importance of exploiting width in deeper spaces ahead of the match, aiming to establish patterns that would facilitate effective use of the width.

    According to recent reports, the half-space players in the 2-3-2-3 system, Bergvall and Maddison, made dynamic movements into the wider areas, made possible by Hoffenheim’s first pressing line. The goal was to create shorter connections for the center-backs to progress into the wide areas. Complementing this, the full-backs, Porro and Gray, deliberately positioned themselves to bind Hoffenheim’s wide players, Hložek and Becker, in the half-space, thereby providing more space and time for Tottenham’s wide players.

    Industry observers note that hoffenheim responded solidly, especially through clear handovers. The central midfielder, in this case, Becker, would situationally take over the full-back, allowing the wide player to shift into the wide areas. However, Maddison could have made more of the side pressing angle from Hložek in some situations. By turning directly forward, he could have bypassed the pressure from the first line and, alongside Son, created a 2v1 against Kadeřábek. This option, however, was rarely utilized.

    Son repeatedly dropped deeper, pulling Kadeřábek out of the defensive line, but this often led to a lack of consistent height occupation for Tottenham. As a result, many progression opportunities—especially down the left side—remained ineffective. Although Hoffenheim’s attempts to push the full-backs wide created space in the half-space, Porro did exploit these opportunities successfully in a few instances, but overall, he did so too rarely to create sustained attacking dynamics. Richarlison could also have moved into these spaces more frequently in the opening phase to strengthen the attacking rhythm.

    Sources indicate that in general, one positive aspect was the consistent use of layoff play on the right build-up side, with Porro tucking inside. Bergvall, who positioned himself wide, highlighted excellent awareness of the game situations under pressure from the opposition. He rapidly recognized that Stach was marking Porro loosely, which allowed Bergvall to frequently find Porro in the center. This situation was well exploited, leading to effective one-two patterns and significantly supporting the build-up structure on the right side.

    Tottenham’s Half-Space Positioning and Defensive Weaknesses.

    A recurring pattern for Tottenham was the positioning of the half-space players. They often remained in their usual positions, staying in the half-space rather than fully occupying the width, but frequently aligning with Bentancur, which resulted in a 2-5-3 system. This setup was often accompanied by deeper, but wide, movements from Kulusevski and Son.

    Industry observers note that due to the binding of Hložek and Bischof by Tottenham’s half-space players, Hoffenheim found it difficult to transfer the ball into the wide areas in a ball-oriented manner. Instead, they were forced to play out through the full-backs, which revealed weaknesses in the ball-oriented shifting of their defensive line. This resulted in large gaps, which Tottenham sought to exploit through quick vertical movements, especially in the half-space. Bergvall in particular pushed forward several times, but tended to do so too quickly, making it difficult for Kulusevski to receive the ball in these patterns. Nsoki, however, defended man-to-man and was able to largely isolate Bergvall’s movements.

    Overall, Kulusevski struggled, particularly under the pressure exerted by Kramarić’s pressing, which intensified the pressure. Return passes to the defensive line were consistently denied. Kulusevski had noticeable difficulty, especially with his first touch, to escape these tight situations.

    It has been revealed that an additional factor was that Kulusevski was often forced to turn using his weaker foot. Combined with the double pressure from Hoffenheim, this led to significant problems in ball control, making it difficult for him to find Bergvall diagonally in the half-space.

    2-0 and 50% Possession at Halftime.

    By the end of the first half, Hoffenheim had only partially been able to capitalize on Tottenham’s initial struggles. What stood out most was that the characteristic pressing through the strikers became less frequent, as Bentancur shifted closer to the ball, increasingly binding the ball-near striker, which led to a noticeable decrease in the intensity of the overall pressing. This change allowed Tottenham to play more return passes and initiate latest build-up attempts without being under constant pressure.

    Industry observers note that additionally, Son was regularly placed in 1v1 situations in the final third towards the end of the half, which naturally created dynamics—helped by some unfortunate defensive actions from Kadeřábek. Furthermore, Richarlison and Maddison often found space in the in-between lines. The large gaps in Hoffenheim’s 4-4-2 system offered Tottenham the opportunity to target these players and create additional dynamics in their offensive play.

    According to recent reports, despite the early lead and a 2-0 score before halftime, Tottenham had just over 50% possession against Hoffenheim by the end of the first half. This surprisingly low figure was partly due to the disjointed nature of the game: many ball losses and fouls characterized the match, with Hoffenheim particularly focusing on physical intensity in the half-space. Additionally, Tottenham showed general problems with coordination and connections between players. Notably, the lack of ball flow was apparent: passes often went astray, and there were difficulties with the first touch— a crucial disadvantage, especially for a style of play that heavily relies on width and time advantages along the sidelines.

    According to recent reports, through the 2-5-3 (or 2-3-5 in the final third), Tottenham also revealed significant weaknesses in their counter-pressing. This was primarily due to ball losses occurring frequently in the wide areas, with surrounding players often moving away from the ball. As a result, there was a lack of necessary ball concentration near the ball, making an effective, pressing-oriented counter-pressing difficult to execute, forcing Tottenham to frequently fall back instead.

    In Hoffenheim’s build-up play under Ilzer in the first half, a clear game proposal was evident: instead of a short build-up, they focused almost entirely on long ball distribution.

    Sources indicate that in principle, the team played out of a 2-3-5 formation, with Kadeřábek and Jurasec positioned more centrally in the second build-up line, but occasionally shifting wide. Stach operated centrally between them, while Becker frequently advanced from the back line and occasionally dropped into the intermediate spaces.

    The extreme overload of the back line was closely linked to Max Moerstedt, who acted as the target player. The striker regularly drifted to the left side, positioning himself close to Porro in order to receive long balls. Around him, three players—usually Bischof, Kramarić, and another teammate—positioned themselves to ensure that the area around the ball was well occupied.

    The central problem with this approach, however, was the overly tight positioning of the players around Moerstedt. The second balls often ended up in more distant zones (green zone), areas that Tottenham could access well from their 4-4-2/5-3-2 structure. Notably, the wide players Son and Kulusevski frequently shifted excellently into these spaces, leading to dangerous counter-attacking situations.

    Both goals conceded in the first half resulted from ball losses in these zones, which Hoffenheim failed to protect effectively. Tottenham’s quick transitions and precise vertical play made the problems with the long ball distribution clearly visible.

    Industry observers note that in general, Moerstedt had a rather unsuccessful day with the long balls. While the balls were often played back towards Baumann intentionally, these passes frequently lacked precision. Additionally, both Porro and Drăgușin were extremely dominant in aerial duels on this occasion.

    It has been revealed that sending Moerstedt into an aerial duel within a densely populated zone also assumes that the team maintains a certain depth behind the target player. However, Hoffenheim failed to establish this depth adequately, resulting in second balls rarely being secured in the deeper areas.

    Industry observers note that during the first month of the season, three players have separated themselves at the top: Yaxel Lendeborg, Cameron Boozer, and Darius Acuff Jr. While it's not a guarantee one of those players wins it, if the season ended today, those would be the top vote-getters.

    Darryn Peterson and AJ Dybantsa — the first two picks of the 2026 NBA Draft — have some ground to make up during the next four months to get back in the mix.

    With the regular season almost a quarter of the way complete, let's dive into our first Rookie of the Year rankings. All odds via FanDuel.

    With Steph Curry out, Lendeborg has continued to step up. He is shooting 48.6% from the field and 41.4% from 3. Lendeborg didn't start shooting 3s on a consistent basis until he got to Michigan last season, so knocking down that percentage on 5.4 attempts per night is a positive sign. Fourteen games into the season, Lendeborg is the favorite.

Boozer keeps getting better and better as a processor as he continues to log more minutes. The Grizzlies have been one of the league's surprising teams this season. Boozer deserves a ton of credit for that. He wins everywhere he goes, whether at the high school, college, or professional level.

    Acuff just turned 20 last week. In 13 games as a teenager, he averaged 25.5 points per game and became the first teenager in NBA history to score at least 275 points and dish out 80 assists in his first 11 games. Acuff is a special offensive talent who is being asked to do more than any rookie in his class. Sacramento is a very bad basketball team, but Acuff makes the Kings somewhat fun to watch. That's a huge credit to him.

    The Jazz have been decimated by injuries this season and are currently riding a 12-game losing streak. The one bright side amidst some very bad basketball is how good Peterson has been during that stretch. Peterson had a five-game stretch in which he scored 20 points in each game and shot the ball well from 3. Peterson is the future of Utah's franchise, so getting him as many reps as possible on and off the ball should be the priority.

    Dybantsa, the No. 1 overall pick, is averaging 14 shot attempts per game during his first 10 appearances as a pro. He should be taking even more shots. The way the Wizards are using him is confusing at times. Dybantsa is in somewhat of a weird situation because of the Wizards' roster.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Philadelphia 76ers are off to a fantastic start to the 2026-27 season at 12-3, good for first in the Eastern Conference, and perhaps most encouraging for the Sixers is that they're winning without looking like a team playing at its absolute peak.

    After a huge offseason adding LeBron James and Jaylen Brown, the Sixers still look like a team figuring out how best to work together, but when it comes time in the fourth quarter to find a way to win, they manage to get the job done. Tyrese Maxey is leading the way with Brown swiftly finding his rhythm, but James and Joel Embiid in particular still seem to be feeling it out early in the season.

    James, who has never averaged less than 20.9 points per game in his previous 23 seasons, is averaging just 15.1 points per game and his 44.3/22.5/71.7 shooting splits are all career lows or close to it. As James figures things out, ESPN reported that a Sixers source claimed James "asked coaches to be patient with him as he expects to find his rhythm and get his conditioning in line by December as he ramps up.".

    That report hit social media and caught James' attention, with the 41-year-old star denying ever saying that.

    According to recent reports, ESPN didn't report a direct quote from James, and it's very possible the Sixers source offered an anecdote that paraphrased James and used the word patience when James never did. That then ended up on a social media graphic and prompted James to shoot it down.

    What's fascinating here is it's not a scathing report or even anything particularly juicy. James is struggling with his shot early in the year and seems to be figuring out exactly where he fits in the offense alongside Maxey, Brown and Embiid as a scorer. He's still doing plenty of things well -- including leading the team with 6.9 assists per game and just took over third all-time in assists in NBA history -- and the Sixers are still winning even with James ice cold with his jumper, which history suggests will turn around at some point.

    Patience would be prudent from the Sixers with James, whether he wants to use that word or not, and it seems like a matter of when, not if, he gets shots to start falling and the Philly offense becomes even more dynamic.

    Industry News: What's next for Red Sox after Jake Bauers deal? Plus more intel from the MLB GM Meetings

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, LAS VEGAS — Uncertainty permeated the ARIA Resort & Casino throughout this week's MLB GM Meetings.
    • 1  approaching, media, executives, and all within the baseball industry had some questions: what would baseball look like once the inevitable lockout goes into place?
    • For the Red Sox, a small piece of this peculiar period centers on what to do with former top prospect Kristian Campbell.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, LAS VEGAS — Uncertainty permeated the ARIA Resort & Casino throughout this week's MLB GM Meetings. The looming lockout, of course, played a major role in all of this.

    With Dec. 1  approaching, media, executives, and all within the baseball industry had some questions: what would baseball look like once the inevitable lockout goes into place? What will it look like once it returns? How do you build a roster with such indeterminacy?

    For the Red Sox, a small piece of this peculiar period centers on what to do with former top prospect Kristian Campbell.

    Tuesday (Nov. 17) is a significant date, marking the deadline for teams to decide which players to protect from the Rule 5 draft by adding them to their 40-man roster. Campbell, who did not appear in a massive-league game in 2026, is currently on the 40-man, signing an eight-year $60 million extension just eight games into his 2025 rookie campaign. But after his demotion in late June of that season, Campbell never found his way back to the majors.

    Now, with the lockout upon baseball, according to one source familiar with the situation, Campbell's 40-man spot might be in jeopardy.

    It has been revealed that boston is weighing the possibility of designating Campbell for assignment. When Craig Breslow, the Sox's president of baseball operations, was asked about that Tuesday, he brushed aside the question.

    In a recent development, "I'm not going to speak to that right now," he mentioned "Kristian's part of our organization. We're really happy about that, and we are invested in doing everything we can to get him to perform like he's capable of.".

    Now, if the Red Sox do DFA Campbell, the belief is that he would clear waivers, given his contract and lackluster performance at the minor-league level. Campbell is owed $55 million over the next six seasons, earning $13 million and $16 million over the 2031 and 2032 seasons, respectively. Campbell posted a .256/.383/.380 slash line with eight homers in 462 plate appearances at Triple-A in 2026.

    According to recent reports, because of those figures, one league executive suggested during the GM Meetings that their club would have no interest in Campbell. The exec took it a step further, confidently suggesting that they couldn't envision any team claiming the outfielder, considering the contract.

    Industry observers note that hypothetically, if Campbell is DFA'd, the Red Sox would free up a 40-man roster spot. If he clears waivers, Campbell, who has less than a year of MLB service time, would be outrighted to Triple-A Worcester. The Red Sox could then eventually add him back to the 40-man roster once they feel his production is worthy of another promotion to the parent club.

    None of this would provide the Red Sox with any financial relief unless another team were to claim him. Campbell's contract would still count toward their competitive balance tax payroll even if he were removed from the 40-man roster and remained in the minors.

    Recent findings suggest that the risk-reward of such a move is something the Red Sox will also have to consider. Campbell has already acknowledged losing confidence following his recent struggles at both the major- and minor-league levels.

    It has been revealed that "He's got a world of potential," said Breslow. "We saw it in the minor leagues when he was coming up. We saw it in the first part of the season in [2025]. Then I think we started to see it in the second half last year, too, [at Worcester]. I still feel like he has a really bright big-league career ahead of him, and excited to get into spring training and see that manifest on the field.".

    The Red Sox signed Jake Bauers to a four-year, $58 million deal Friday, giving the club another power bat in their lineup. Willson Contreras will continue to anchor first base while Bauers will serve as the primary DH, filling in for Contreras from time to time.

    It has been revealed that bauers had a breakout season with the Brewers this year, batting .266/.389/.484 with an .874 OPS and 26 homers. The combo of plate discipline and damage in the strike zone intrigued the Red Sox. Furthermore, his ability to lift the ball in the air and use the entire field despite being a lefty gives the Red Sox confidence that he will be productive at Fenway.

    Recent findings suggest that with Bauers part of the fold, though, Jarren Duran's future with the club is even more murky. The Sox are a heavily left-handed offensive club with Bauers, Wilyer Abreu, Masataka Yoshida, Roman Anthony, and Duran in the mix.

    Sources indicate that one is likely going to have to go. And Duran, who could earn upwards of $11 million in arbitration next season, appears to be the most likely to be dealt.

    Even before the Bauers signing, multiple sources suggested during the GM Meetings that both the Red Sox and Duran might be better off parting ways via trade.

    Naturally, there is some apprehension.

    Industry observers note that "I've been hearing for three years now about the outfield logjam that we have, but the reality is we haven't had all of our outfielders, including Masataka, healthy at the same time," Breslow mentioned. "These things have largely taken care of themselves, unfortunately.".

    #61924. Industry News: Organized Chaos: Bournemouth’s Possession Principles Against Nottingham – MH

    Industry News: Organized Chaos: Bournemouth’s Possession Principles Against Nottingham – MH

    📅 28 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 28.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League,Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren.
    • On Matchday 23, the two surprise teams of the Premier League faced off.
    • It has been revealed that bournemouth’s coach, Andoni Iraola, is a former player under Marcelo Bielsa at Athletic Bilbao.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 28.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League,Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren.

    On Matchday 23, the two surprise teams of the Premier League faced off. Nottingham, unbeaten in their last nine matches, has impressed this season with outstanding defensive work. Bournemouth, coached by Andoni Iraola and now unbeaten in 12 games, takes a completely different tactical approach compared to most other teams. In an interview with TNT Sports, Guardiola remarked: “Today, modern football is the way Bournemouth, Newcastle, Brighton, and Liverpool play.” What exactly are these teams doing differently? Bournemouth’s approach will be analyzed in detail based on this match.

    It has been revealed that bournemouth’s coach, Andoni Iraola, is a former player under Marcelo Bielsa at Athletic Bilbao. Bielsa, widely known in the Premier League as the coach who led Leeds United to promotion, gained recognition for his style of play characterized by exceptionally high intensity in all phases of the game. According to Iraola, his own footballing philosophy has been significantly shaped by his former coach Bielsa.

    In an interview with Sky, back when he was still managing Rayo Vallecano, Iraola stated: “I was very lucky to play for him (Bielsa) for two seasons as a player. I think he has another vision of football. They were two very good seasons for us, and, for me, it was a different knowledge.” He also explained: “I use a lot of exercises from Marcelo that I learned from him. I use a lot of things, especially with the ball. Offensively, his teams are very dynamic. He is willing to make all the runs to the space, he is ready to accept this kind of disorder, offensively.”.

    Iraola’s tactical concept can be described as “organized chaos.” The aim is not to implement a positional system with perfect patterns of play. Instead, the focus is on creating problems for opposing teams by generating chaos. The idea is to force the opponent into unfamiliar, uncontrolled phases of play. A particularly notable concept within this is highly intense, man-oriented, hybrid attacking pressing, designed to force the opponent into quick turnovers and a fast-paced, direct game.

    According to recent reports, „It is true that we like, and we perform better, in high-tempo games. We need to run a lot. We don’t need so much control, not in every single play, but I think we have the legs, we have the willingness, to go up and down.“ – Iraola.

    According to recent reports, accordingly, Iraola’s style of play could face challenges against deep-lying teams that deliberately thrive on minimal possession. These teams don’t need to engage with Bournemouth’s high-intensity game but can instead remain compact out of possession. They are not required to build up play from the back under Bournemouth’s pressing to maintain controlled possession but can focus on their own offensive transitions. This season, Nottingham has been one of the most successful teams in executing such an approach. Consequently, it was particularly intriguing to observe how Iraola’s Bournemouth would operate in possession against Nottingham’s deep block.

    Iraola describes his philosophy in possession as follows:.

    According to recent reports, “We have to prepare [positional] patterns, but we cannot just prioritise them. If you can see that you don’t have a teammate ahead, forget about the pattern, just drive the ball and try to force things to happen. I want him to attack first.”.

    Sources indicate that here lies the challenge I encountered while analyzing the game against Nottingham: how do you describe intentionally provoked chaos, where there are barely any fixed patterns? Only a few predefined sequences can be identified within the positional framework. The crucial question, therefore, is: what reference points structure Bournemouth’s possession play, and which principles of play create this chaos? Or, put simply: what “tools” does Iraola use in his style of play? To answer this, the positional framework of the game against Nottingham will first be examined.

    Industry observers note that starting from a nominal 4-2-3-1 formation, Nottingham defended out of possession in a 4-4-1-1 or 4-5-1 structure. Nottingham focused primarily on defending and largely conceded possession to Bournemouth, a characteristic approach for the team. Under coach Simoes Espirito Santo, Nottingham has averaged just 40% possession this season.

    Recent findings suggest that bournemouth, meanwhile, operated in possession with a positional 2-4-4 or 2-3-2-3 structure, featuring wide wingers and full-backs. From this setup, Bournemouth attempted to break through Nottingham’s deep block. On the (left) No. 10 position, Kluivert stood out with his exceptional dribbling ability and high agility. Central midfielder Christie alternated between the deeper right half-space as a right-sided No. 10 and the No. 6 position.

    Industry observers note that nottingham was often forced back into their own half from an initially higher defensive pressing. When Nottingham attempted to press higher, Bournemouth’s center-backs positioned themselves wide, and goalkeeper Kepa moved up to form part of the back line. This made it nearly impossible for Nottingham’s lone striker to put significant pressure on the ball carrier. As a result, Nottingham dropped deep, retreated, and refrained from pressing the ball-carrying center-backs.

    It has been revealed that „I sometimes value much more a player carrying the ball and forcing things to happen. I think when you play too positional – one, two touches to find a free man – you sometimes lose the initiative from the players to just take their man on and attack the spaces.” – Iraola.

    This approach meant that Bournemouth’s center-backs were frequently required to dribble forward against stationary opponents, forcing defenders to commit. This often created 5v4 or 4v4 situations on the flanks, caused by the strong lateral movements of striker Ouattara and attacking midfielder Kluivert, combined with the forward dribbling of the center-backs. When no passingoptions were available, the team didn’t rebuild play, as is typical for positionally oriented teams. Instead, Bournemouth’s left center-back, Huijsen, was occasionally seen dribbling directly at the opponent’s last defensive line. It can be concluded that one of Iraola’s key principles of play is to attack vertically with the ball as early as possible.

    Center-back Huijsen dribbles toward the final defensive line himself due to a lack of better-positioned deeper passing options.

    In a recent development, the situations on the flanks during the center-back’s dribbling were played out in various ways. Sometimes the ball was passed to the wide player on the wing, who was tasked with taking on a 1v1 duel. This player was consistently supported by the full-back in a dual-width setup.

    Particularly noteworthy were the positional rotations of the 3-4 players on the flanks. Full-backs, attacking midfielder Kluivert, striker Ouattara, and the winger frequently rotated out of their positions, occupying different spaces. What stood out was the consistent presence of a dynamic deep run within these rotations, forcing the opponent to cover the run and thereby creating space between their players.

    The positional rotations with deep runs create passing options.

    For example, the left-back Kerkez, during the center-back’s dribble, occasionally made deep runs into the half-space. Similarly, attacking midfielder Kluivert was often involved, sometimes shifting laterally to receive the ball and then driving forward at pace to attack the defensive block.

    Nottingham responded to this from the 30th minute by attempting to apply more pressure on Bournemouth’s ball-carrying center-backs. The 4-4-1-1 shape was adjusted by removing the man-marking on defensive midfielder Adams. Instead, Nottingham transitioned into a 4-4-2 setup, aiming to position Adams in the cover shadow and step out earlier to press the center-backs. However, Bournemouth’s goalkeeper Kepa played so high in the back line that he was still able to connect with the now even wider-positioned center-backs, allowing them to continue dribbling forward.

    The goalkeeper stepping into the back line creates a 4v2 situation, allowing the center-backs to dribble forward with less pressure from opponents.

    “I would say they have the freedom to risk a little bit in the dribbles.“ – Iraola.

    Sources indicate that another key principle of Bournemouth’s possession game is diagonal, vertical dribbling. These serve as a chaos factor and are constantly utilized across all positions. As long as no teammate is better positioned toward the opponent’s goal, players are given the freedom to dribble. The skillful dribblers on the wings, the striker, and attacking midfielder Kluivert fit perfectly into this principle. The spaces opened up through the aforementioned rotations, particularly between the opposing players on the flanks, were mostly attacked through dribbling rather than passing.

    The core idea behind this focus on dribbling is closely aligned with the concept of relationism. The goal is to make the team’s decisions less predictable for the opponent and to create a certain degree of chaos. Traditional positional play often limits players’ individual freedom, which reduces the element of surprise. However, Iraola’s execution of possession football differs significantly from relationism.

    Instead of using a tighter structure to encourage combinations between players, rotations and larger distances between players are used to create spaces intended to be attacked through dribbling. It is crucial that these dribbles are always executed as vertical actions, continually putting the opponent under defensive pressure and thereby opening up other options.

    Due to the larger spaces on the flanks, many dribbles are initiated on the wing, supported by the dual-width occupation of the winger and full-back. To enforce a successful follow-up action against deep-lying opponents, proper box occupation is a fundamental requirement. Iraola’s teams often flood the opponent’s penalty area with up to seven players, forcing the opposition right in front of their own goal. The goal is not necessarily to find the open player but to increase the likelihood of winning the ball after a cross in the penalty area. Second balls also play a significant role in this approach.

    Sources indicate that risky dribbles have the additional advantage of provoking more frequent transition moments. When the opponent tries to transition offensively, they lose their compact defensive shape. Bournemouth’s flexible rest defense allows the ball to be immediately recovered after a loss of possession. Bournemouth’s rest defense typically consists of 3-4 players, depending on the attacking structure. In addition to the two center-backs, defensive midfielder Adams and the inverted, far-side full-back provide cover. If both full-backs or Adams are involved in the attack, Christie drops deeper to provide support and shifts closer to the ball.

    On one hand, it’s vital to highlight the excellent sense of positioning from the two central midfielders, Adams and Christie, in anticipating potential turnovers. Their ability to read these moments and their spatial awareness lead to many successful counter-pressing actions. On the other hand, the immediate pressure applied to the ball-carrying opponent after a turnover is notable, leaving the opposition with little opportunity to create controlled possession phases.

    In a recent development, as a result, Nottingham’s offensive presence in the first half was minimal. Successful offensive transitions by Simoes Espirito Santo’s team were extremely rare.

    Recent findings suggest that the rest-defense structure in the 21st minute consists of the inverted Kerkez, the shifting defensive midfielder Adams, and the center-backs. At the same time, the ball-near teammates position themselves in response to the dribble in a way that allows them to immediately apply pressure if needed.

    According to recent reports, another key principle of Bournemouth’s play is that after regaining possession, the first action is immediately directed forward. In contrast to traditionally positional teams, control is not sought through possession in chaotic situations but rather through constant transitions. The goal is to prevent the opponent from regaining their structure and settling into their usual rhythm. This creates intense pressure for Bournemouth’s opponents. As a result, Bournemouth often didn’t even need to break down Nottingham’s defensive block because the opponent never had the chance to regain their typical structure.

    After recovering the ball, Bournemouth consistently looked to play forward into pressure. When positioned deeper (closer to their own goal), players in the forward zones immediately made runs into space to create vertical passing options. Even if the Bournemouth player who regained the ball was immediately under pressure, the first action was directed forward.

    Industry observers note that if necessary, a long ball was played toward the opponent’s defensive line, with a focus on winning second balls. This pressing game with an emphasis on second balls—often referred to as “kick and rush”—generated additional forced transition situations, preventing the opponent from finding their usual shape. The fact that four of Bournemouth’s five goals against the typically deep-lying Nottingham team came from deliberately provoked transition moments highlights the effectiveness of this approach.

    In the second half, Nottingham switched to an attacking press in an attempt to create more scoring opportunities and overturn the 1-0 deficit. However, Nottingham was unable to pin Bournemouth in their own half as planned. Instead, Bournemouth played targeted long balls to one of their four advanced attackers or to the half-high positioned full-backs. Through a combination of winning second balls, dribbles, and central midfielders following up for lay-offs, Bournemouth was able to rapidly progress into space and control the game from their own half. This led to Bournemouth scoring their second and third goals in quick succession. The final result was a resounding 5-0 victory for Iraola’s side.

    It has been revealed that so, what exactly causes the chaos in Bournemouth’s possession play? In summary, it is a combination of the principles discussed: playing vertically as early as possible; dribbling diagonally and vertically as long as no player is better positioned toward the opponent’s goal; and making the first action after regaining possession a forward one. The focus on vertical zones (reference point: opponent players) and second balls (reference point: the opponent’s goal) creates an intense and dynamic style of play that prevents the opponent from settling into their usual structure. Bournemouth is further aided by their attacking press, which was not analyzed in detail in this article but consistently provokes additional transition situations.

    What can other teams take away from Bournemouth’s possession approach without abandoning their own philosophy? One lesson is the courage to consistently seek depth, provided the team has appropriate counter-pressing structures in place. Additionally, the dynamism of individual actions at Bournemouth is remarkable. Rarely have I seen such explosive runs into depth from other teams.

    It has been revealed that the final question is: what do the teams mentioned by Guardiola in the aforementioned interview have in common? All of them attack the depth quickly and frequently, making the game incredibly dynamic and intense. This forces the opponent to make decisions faster. After all, the main difference between good and very good players is the time it takes to make a good decision.

    According to recent reports, my recommendation is to watch games from 30 years ago. It quickly becomes apparent that football has become faster and more demanding.

    “For me, the players are better than in 2003. They have to do the same things, but much faster. The physical demands are ridiculous. I doubt I could have played at this rhythm.” – Iraola.

    Breaking: NBA MVP Rankings: Luka Dončić, Victor Wembanyama in a two-horse race; Stephen Curry's absence speaks volumes

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We're nearly a month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and while some people say it's too early to start talking about MVP, we are not among those people.
    • According to recent reports, right now, it's a clear two-horse race: Luka Doncic or Victor Wembanyama?
    • The Luka Dončić we're watching right now isn't just the best offensive player in the world.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We're nearly a month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and while some people say it's too early to start talking about MVP, we are not among those people.

    According to recent reports, right now, it's a clear two-horse race: Luka Doncic or Victor Wembanyama? There is a real split on this. Here's where I stand as of Tuesday, Nov. 17.

    The Luka Dončić we're watching right now isn't just the best offensive player in the world. He might be the best in history. Nobody has ever put up anything close to the numbers he is charting at the moment: 39 points per game with seven assists, seven boards, nearly two steals and a positively scorching 66.0 TS%, the latter being a number even the great Stephen Curry has only bested twice in his career.

    Recent findings suggest that it's early, sure. Dončić isn't likely to keep making 3s at this rate for an entire season, and indeed we've seen some slippage of late (35% over his last four, if you really want to split hairs), but his volume remains, with 4.5 makes a night over that stretch. Dončić remains on track to break Curry's single-season record of 402 3-pointers, and he's done more off-ball shooting than in the past.

    Throw in more transition production and a 53% midrange conversion rate, per Cleaning The Glass, and you're seeing a more diverse scorer, which is to say this isn't just a guy who has started off hot on his step-back 3s (though this is a major factor, too, of course), but a guy piercing defenses from more spots with different shots. If Dončić could actually be any harder to guard than he has been in the past, we're seeing it this season.

    He's also defending. His 23 steals rank sixth league-wide. Only two players have recovered more defensive loose balls than his eight. Only one has taken more charges than his four. With Dončić as the primary defender, shooters are converting just 36.7% of their shots against a 45.1 expected FG%; that minus-8.6 is the fourth-largest discrepancy among all players who've contested at least 150 shots.

    Industry observers note that most importantly, the Lakers are 12-2 and tied with the Spurs atop the Western Conference. The Lakers rank as the league's top offense with a rating that balloons to 129.2 points per 100 possessions (which would be an NBA record by a long shot) with Dončić on, and a net rating, as illustrated below, that falls off a cliff when he sits.

    Look, if you have Wembanyama ahead of Dončić in the MVP race a month into the season, nobody is going to argue much with you. The oddsmakers slightly favor Wembanyama (+110 at FanDuel; Dončić is +140), who, as you'll see below, has what would qualify as a potentially unanimous case in most years. But this isn't most years. We got a dude averaging nearly 40 points for a No. 1 seed that nobody expected to be a No. 1 seed. Until one of those things changes, it's hard for me to go against Dončić.

    If you think Dončić's plus-35.5 on/off split (it's actually plus-32.2 without filtering for garbage time) is crazy, have a look at Wembanyama's number.

    Victor Wembanyama's impact this season has been another level. Spurs are +42.6 points per 100 possessions with Wemby on the court than off it, according to @cleantheglass. Small sample but other-worldly. Lakers star Luka Dončić is at +35.5 pts/100 poss.Both numbers are better… pic.twitter.com/0GJCFFmZ5K.

    Industry observers note that yes, you're reading that right. The Spurs, for all their supportive talent, fall by 42.6 points per 100 possessions when Wembanyama leaves the court (plus-29.2 on vs. minus-13.3 off), per Cleaning the Glass. By comparison, the best on/off split that Nikola Jokić has ever recorded is plus-24.8. Curry's best is plus-21.3. LeBron James' is plus-17.8. Go down that list and look at the most impactful on-off splits those guys have ever posted. Wembanyama is in another galaxy.

    Industry observers note that and it's key to note that Wembanyama plays on a great team, as all these guys in the graphic have. The fact that there is still so much difference between when Wembanyama is on the court and when he isn't, even in a small sample, is honestly difficult to comprehend. San Antonio's three-guard lineup was supposed to be an experiment, but it's hard to know if Dylan Harper, De'Aaron Fox and Stephon Castle truly optimize one another or if Wembanyama is enough to make any lineup dominant in spite of traditional issues (like none of those three being a true shooter).

    In a recent development, wembanyama is the best defensive player on the planet by an immeasurable amount. Even the stats don't do it justice. He's on pace for north of 350 blocks, a number only four players (Elmore Smith, Mark Eaton, Manute Bol and Hakeem Olajuwon) have eclipsed since blocks became an official stat in 1973, and still it's just as much, if not more, about the shots he deters scorers from even attempting.

    It has been revealed that and why would they? Scorers are making just 33.6% of their shots when Wembanyama is the nearest defender, a 17% drop from their expected 50.4%. That also leads the league among all players who've defended at least 120 shots, and again, it fails to fully capture his defensive dominance.

    The fact that we've gotten this far without talking about Wembanyama's offense, as if it's a mere afterthought for a guy to be averaging 28.6 points and 11.6 rebounds in under 30 minutes a night. Wembanyama is figuring out his hot spots, prioritizing closer-to-the-basket positioning where he is a skyscraper among regular NBA buildings. He's taking two more paint shots per game than he did last season; 43% of his shots are coming from inside four feet, per Cleaning the Glass, up from 38% last season, and his 4.6 dunks per game (up from 2.7 last year) have him on pace to shatter Rudy Gobert's single-season record of 306.

    Recent findings suggest that if I had to guess, Wembanyama's production is more sustainable than Dončić's. It's hard to imagine Dončić not hitting a rough patch from 3, and he's almost certainly not going to keep scoring 39 points per game. He'll be over 35 points per game when everything is remarked and done because that's what the Lakers need from him, but there's a burnout factor while Wembanyama is kind of cruising to these numbers, and the defensive impact is as natural as breathing. My gut says Wembanyama will be a clearer MVP favorite by Christmas.

    Assuming Dončić and Wembanyama each get to the mandated 65 games, everyone else is playing for third place at the moment. Which is crazy given the seasons some of the following names are having.

    According to recent reports, one of two players averaging at least 22 points, nine rebounds and seven assists, and the only player to be leading his team in all three categories. The Rockets are 11-4 with the No. 2 offense and Sengun is the center of it all.

    Tatum is averaging his normal 26.5 points per game. The shooting efficiency still hasn't come around, but he is an absolute quarterback on this Celtics team. He draws the doubles, and his 35.1% assist rate, per CTG, is a career high by a mile. The Celtics, for my money, are the best team in the East.

    Cunningham is, once again, doing everything for the Pistons, who have been without Jalen Duren for all but the first four games and are still a top-three East seed. The 3-point shooting is down, but that's splitting hairs. This guy is shot-creating machine and, as forceful as he plays, he makes it look as smooth as anyone in the league.

    According to recent reports, here come the Heat, who have won five straight games, with the last three wins coming over the Cavaliers, Pistons and Rockets. Antetokounmpo is averaging 28.3/12.5/5.2 with 1.3 blocks per game on 60% shooting. He's on fire from the midrange as the Heat are exploiting the soft spots in all the drop coverage they're facing.

    Gilgeous-Alexander has so much on his plate that it actually creates a clearer path to a third straight MVP if he can somehow lift Oklahoma City above all these injuries. He's trying. The Thunder are 9-5 and he's getting his 30.9 points per game, but his 58.7 true-shooting is down considerably, which makes sense as he has to force tougher shots now with fewer weapons around him.

    Industry observers note that curry's value can perhaps be felt most in his absence. The Warriors have lost three straight since he went out with a torn oblique, the last two by 59 points. The Warriors have outscored opponents by 13.5 points per 100 possessions with Curry on the floor this season and have been outscored by 8.3 points per 100 possessions without him. Along with Yaxel Lendeborg, who's being asked as a rookie to carry an impossibly heavy weight without Curry, Curry remains the only real lifeblood of a team that is still shockingly lifeless without him.

    Breaking: Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

    📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey.
    • Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era.
    • Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

    Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

    Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

    Industry observers note that kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

    In a recent development, it's notable to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

    According to recent reports, right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

    Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

    Industry observers note that we already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

    It has been revealed that however, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

    With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

    Recent findings suggest that it was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

    Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

    Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

    Sources indicate that utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

    Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

    Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

    Sources indicate that with the General Manager Meetings now in the rearview mirror, it sure seems like we're playing out the clock in Major League Baseball news until the CBA expires. That would be Dec. 1 at 11:59 p.m. ET. The expectation at this juncture is that the owners will lock the players out and we'll deal with several months of public negotiations. Until then, we can hope to see some player movement, such as the Red Sox signing Jake Bauers.

    In the meantime, let's round up the news and rumors for the day.

    The Padres are in desperate need of starting pitching, should they wish to continue contending. The rotation right now would be Joe Musgrove, Randy Vásquez, JP Sears, Jhony Brito and a shrugging emoji. Sure enough, they are all over the rumor mill for rotation help.

    Industry observers note that the San Diego Union-Tribune reports that they've shown interest in "virtually every starting pitcher" in free agency, "from Tarik Skubal on down. From Matthew Boyd to Shota Imanaga to Dustin May to Kaima Taira." Further, ESPN reports that the Padres have a meeting set up with Skubal but have also shown interest in Freddy Peralta, as well as Michael King, Nick Pivetta and Nick Martinez.

    Expect them to remain active until they land at least two starters.

    It's no secret that the Diamondbacks are open to trading All-Star second baseman Ketel Marte. The Blue Jays have been sniffing around, and now the Orioles have emerged as a suitor, per MLB.com.

    According to recent reports, this one is interesting in that it's not a natural fit. The Orioles have extra infielders and have been noted to be shopping infielders in order to land outfield help. Between second and third base, the Orioles have Jackson Holliday, Jordan Westburg, Blaze Alexander, Coby Mayo and Christian Encarnacion-Strand. Presumably, if they are able to swing a deal for Marte, there would be some shuffling with more trades and/or moving someone to the outfield.

    The Mets could have an opening at first base as things currently stand and they've checked in on free agent Ty France, according to the Newly introduced York Post.

    Currently, the Mets are looking at Jared Young (coming off a scary head injury), Mark Vientos and Jorge Polanco as options at first base.

    Sources indicate that france, 32 and probably considered a journeyman at this point, had a major season in 2026 for the Padres. He hit .295/.363/.502 (139 OPS+) with 21 homers, 72 RBI and a career-high 4.5 WAR.

    Recent findings suggest that reliever Jonathan Loáisiga is close to signing with a new team, reports ESPN. The Dodgers are among five teams involved, with the New York Post adding the Phillies, Mets, Yankees and Blue Jays to the mix.

    In 67 outings last season for Arizona, Loáisiga pitched to a 2.42 ERA, 1.03 WHIP and had 48 strikeouts in 67 innings.

    Recent findings suggest that the Yankees have re-signed left-handed reliever Tim Hill to a one-year, $2.25 million deal with a $2.5 million club option for 2028, per ESPN. Hill, 36, made 67 appearances last season with a 4.60 ERA, 1.14 WHIP and 25 strikeouts in 58 ⅔ innings. He held lefties to a .213/.265/.346 line.

    Everton dispatch Newcastle to give Matthias Jaissle a reality check

    📅 12 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Everton appear well ahead of Newcastle United in their preparation for the new Premier League season after a comfortable 3-1 victory at Murrayfield.
    • On a sobering evening for latest Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle, who changed all 10 outfield players at half-time, Everton’s one and two-touch attacking play proved difficult to contain.
    • Everton took the lead through Thierno Barry after a defensive error from Sven Botman, before Iliman Ndiaye scored a penalty that was won cheaply by summer signing Hayden Hackney.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Everton appear well ahead of Newcastle United in their preparation for the new Premier League season after a comfortable 3-1 victory at Murrayfield.

    On a sobering evening for latest Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle, who changed all 10 outfield players at half-time, Everton’s one and two-touch attacking play proved difficult to contain.

    Everton took the lead through Thierno Barry after a defensive error from Sven Botman, before Iliman Ndiaye scored a penalty that was won cheaply by summer signing Hayden Hackney.

    Newcastle’s raft of half-time changes helped David Moyes’s team strengthen their grip further, with Tyrique George adding a stylish third and 19-year-old Harrison Armstrong providing his second assist of the game.

    Among the Newcastle players introduced at half-time was 18-year-old Sean Steur, the exciting midfield prospect signed from Ajax this summer. Aladji Bamba and Bazoumana Toure also flickered with promise, but a sharp start from Jaissle’s team faded.

    They pulled a goal back late on when Jacob Murphy’s cross found Harvey Barnes at the back post, but they offered little as an attacking force throughout the second half.

    Newcastle have two more friendlies, against Bayer Leverkusen and Strasbourg, before they begin their Premier League season at home to Liverpool.

    The club are reeling from the summer departures of Bruno Guimaraes, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and manager Eddie Howe, but David Hopkinson, the chief executive, struck a bullish tone when he spoke of this being the start of “Newcastle 2.0”.

    Everton look the more settled side and club, and the performances of upcoming arrivals Hackney and George were encouraging, while Thierno Barry was sharp in the centre-forward position that has proved so difficult for the club to fill in recent seasons.

    Everton kick-off their newly introduced season at home to Crystal Palace, and keeping Ndiaye at the club beyond the end of the transfer window will be a priority.

    The scoreline is a fair reflection of the game. Everton looked sharper, as well as fitter, and there are more positives for them to take. They look ready for the latest season, Newcastle need reinforcements.

    Alcaraz bends a shot not far wide from 25 yards for Everton. The game is meandering towards its conclusion now.

    Willock collects the ball between the lines, feeds Murphy wide right, and his ball across goal is turned in at the back post by Harvey Barnes.

    Moyes makes another pair of changes: Keane and Hackney off, O’Brien and Foster on.

    Everton fans are enjoying themselves now, belting out Spirit of the Blues at Murrayfield.

    According to recent reports, more defending for Newcastle to do but they deal with Hackney’s corner delivery. All too easy for Everton to slice through their midfield in the build up though.

    That goal had been coming, and Tyrique George is heavily involved again. He carries the ball forward and finds Armstrong, who returns the favour. George shoots on the swivel and picks out the bottom corner.

    Industry observers note that if I were a Newcastle fan in the stands, Edinbugh’s city centre hostelries would be looking very alluring just about now. There is not much for them to watch in this season half, they are chasing shadows. Some of that can be put down to the handful of young plyers in their second-half XI.

    Tyler Dribbling drops a shoulder down the right, and wins a corner off Harvey Barnes. Everton are finishing this game the stronger, there are more goals in this should they put their foot on the pedal.

    Sources indicate that newcastle, with some youngsters in their defence, looking a little ragged against Everton’s direct attacks now, but George runs into traffic at the edge of the box. Then Alcaraz is booked for a cynical foul.

    Three more Everton changes on the way: Beto, Dibling and Alcaraz on for Barry, Ndiaye and Dewsbury-Hall.

    Hayden Hackney plays a one-two with Tyrique George for Everton, with the former Chelsea winger backheeling the ball into Hackney’s path, and there were unheeded calls for a penalty. It was more of a penalty than the one Everton were awarded in the first half, Lewis Miley tripped him.

    Industry observers note that thierno Barry’s performance has been a positive for Everton, could he nail down the No 9 role this season? It has been a problem position for several seasons now. Barry is tripped and Everton have a free-kick.

    How Aidan Hutchinson injury could grant Lions a salary cap credit in 2027

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The loss of star edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson, who suffered a season-ending torn ACL while celebrating a sack in Week 10, is a brutal blow to the Detroit Lions in their hunt for the NFC North title and beyond.
    • In the massive four-year, $180 million contract extension Hutchinson signed in 2025, there is a clause that permits the Lions to purchase insurance policies against his salary, according to the Detroit Free Press.
    • The contract reportedly states that the Lions are entitled to purchase insurance policies naming them as beneficiaries for up to $60 million in lost salary if Hutchinson cannot play due to injury.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The loss of star edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson, who suffered a season-ending torn ACL while celebrating a sack in Week 10, is a brutal blow to the Detroit Lions in their hunt for the NFC North title and beyond. There is a silver lining to the injury, though. Clauses in Hutchinson's contract and the NFL's collective bargaining agreement with the NFL Players Association open the door for the Lions to potentially gain financial flexibility as a result of his looming absence.

    In the massive four-year, $180 million contract extension Hutchinson signed in 2025, there is a clause that permits the Lions to purchase insurance policies against his salary, according to the Detroit Free Press.

    The contract reportedly states that the Lions are entitled to purchase insurance policies naming them as beneficiaries for up to $60 million in lost salary if Hutchinson cannot play due to injury. For this season specifically, the Lions may insure up to $45 million. That sum includes $15 million of his signing bonus, the full $28.4 million option bonus and his $1.2 million base salary.

    It is unknown whether the Lions purchased those policies and, if so, whether they maximized them.

    Not only would the Lions earn a prorated amount of Hutchinson's salary as an insurance payment, but the CBA would also allow them to receive salary cap credits in future years to offset the difference between Hutchinson's pay and the insurance proceeds.

    Industry observers note that hutchinson's salary and bonuses still count toward the 2026 salary cap, but the Lions could free up millions of dollars in space for 2027 if they purchased sizable insurance policies. According to Over The Cap, Detroit owns the fourth-most cap space this year at $32.9 million and ninth most in 2027 at $62.1 million. Multiple key players, including tight end Sam LaPorta and safety Brian Branch, will reach free agency at the end of this season, so maximizing 2027 cap space would help the Lions re-sign them to larger contracts.

    Recent findings suggest that salary insurance is expensive, and the Lions do not purchase policies for all players. They reportedly did not insure quarterback Jared Goff's contract when he inked an extension in 2024, nor did they insure linebacker Jack Campbell offseason deal. Campbell suffered a severe neck injury in Week 8, and it is unclear when -- or even if -- he will return to the football field.

    Recent findings suggest that language about salary cap credits for insurance payments first appeared in the CBA in 2006. It took a few years for teams to take advantage of the clause. A CBS Sports report in 2024 found that the Newly introduced York Giants included an insurance clause in the addendum to Eli Manning's historic 2009 contract extension that made him the highest-paid player in the NFL. And the earliest known instance of a team qualifying for the cap credit came in 2013 when the Green Bay Packers insured $20 million of Aaron Rodgers' $35 million signing bonus.

    According to recent reports, the Lions have a history of insuring their largest contracts. They did so in 2017, when they took out a policy on Matthew Stafford's five-year, $135 million extension. Interestingly, they did not do the same when they re-signed Goff. And as of Oct. 2024, Goff's contract was the only one out of the 13 quarterbacks who earned an average of $45 million per year or more that was not insured.

    Salary cap credits tied to these insurance policies tend to be more modest than one might think. The policies typically require players to miss a certain number of games before payouts begin. Sometimes there is a deductible associated with the policy. This reduces the total payout and, in turn, the amount of cap relief teams receive from the NFL.

    Here are a few examples of cap credits teams received as part of their insurance policies:.

    Torn ACL, strained hamstring (15 games).
